newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine says talks on closing Chernobyl going well.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine says talks on closing Chernobyl going well.

text.p: Ukraine has made "great progress" in talks with the West on how to shut down Chernobyl but no final decision has been taken on compensation for the loss of energy, Environment Minister Yuri Kostenko said on Monday.
He was speaking at a news conference after the latest round of talks with Ukraine's partners from the Group of Seven industrialised countries in Washington on February 10-11.
Ukraine's ideas for making the area around the plant safe by stabilising the stricken reactor were not approved unanimously, but "accepted on the whole", he said.
He did not say exactly how the reactor, encased in a cracking concrete sarcophagus, would be stabilised.

Before departing for Washington, Kostenko said Ukraine was no longer considering proposals to build a new sarcophagus, including one put forth by a Franco-British alliance led by Generale des Eaux subsidiary Campenon Bernard SGE and one by German engineering firm Trischler and Partners.
On Monday he said experts would spend three months working out how to remove the fuel from inside reactor number four which exploded in 1986, spouting radiation across much of Europe.
Meanwhile the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), which is to finance the project using G7 money, would soon work out a financial mechanism.
Kostenko confirmed that an EBRD report had found a plan to add an extra reactor each at the Rivne and Khmelnitsky power plants in western Ukraine did not meet its financial criteria.
But he added that it was the bank, and not the writers of the report, that would make the final decision.
He accused the report's authors of failing to take into account the state of Ukraine's struggling energy sector and called its findings "superficial".

"Financing these two stations is a political obligation for the G7 according to the memorandum," he said, referring to a deal signed with the West to shut down Chernobyl by 2000 in return for $3.1 billion in loans and credits.
A major sticking point has been to what extent the former Soviet republic will compensate for the energy lost itself by implementing energy-saving programmes.
Kostenko said it was realistic to say the two plants would be completed by 2000 and Chernobyl shut down by then but not realistic to complete energy-saving projects.

"Unfortunately the commission decided it was better for Ukraine to invest money in giving out loans to every family to use energy-saving technology. This could only be done in 20 to 30 years, not immediately," he said.
He said the two sides would meet again in March and a final decision on funding the shutdown would be taken at a G7 summit in June and then approved by the EBRD's leadership in July.
If negotiations failed, Ukraine would try to find private investment to solve the problem themselves, he said.
Hundreds of thousands of people were forced to leave their homes when the reactor blew up and Ukrainian officials say more than 4,000 deaths can be directly attributed to the blast.
